idiom_name: named durable subscription over a broker-retained backlog (subscription/consumer-group/persistent session)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: register the subscriber with a stable subscription identity on the pub-sub channel and let the messaging infrastructure keep its backlog. On every start, re-attach with the same identity and drain the retained messages - or resume from the committed position - in bounded batches, acknowledging or committing progress only after the handler's side effect is durable. Configure retention explicitly (message expiry, queue or offset quota, offset retention, session expiry) against the longest outage you intend to survive, and treat exhaustion of retention as data loss rather than as a reconnect. Delivery is at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent; a long outage becomes a burst, so catch-up must be batch-bounded and observable through backlog depth or lag.
code_sketch:
sub = channel.register_durable_subscriber(name="billing-ledger", client_id=...)
configure_retention(topic, expiry=..., max_backlog=...)      # aligned to the outage budget
loop:
    batch = sub.receive(max_messages=N, max_wait=T)          # bounded catch-up batch
    for m in batch:
        handle_idempotently(m)                               # side effect first
        sub.acknowledge(m)                                   # then checkpoint progress
    publish_lag_metric(sub.backlog_depth)
pitfalls: Treating durability as delivery: an identity that changes on every deployment (new client id, new group id, ephemeral consumer name) starts from scratch and orphans the old backlog.
Leaving retention at its defaults - most brokers default to short or absent retention - so an outage longer than expected silently loses the messages the pattern was supposed to keep.
Acknowledging before the side effect is durable, which turns at-least-once into at-most-once.

Wrong move: provision a durable backlog for every transient or retired subscriber without a quota or expiry -> per-subscriber storage grows with publish rate and outage duration, and abandoned identities consume broker capacity -> instead assign an owner, bound retention, alert on stored bytes, and delete retired subscriptions.

Wrong move: treat growing consumer lag as harmless because the broker retains messages -> replay bursts can overwhelm the returning consumer or the retention window can expire before catch-up -> instead alert on lag and age, drain in bounded batches, and provision catch-up capacity.

Wrong move: reconnect with a new JMS client id, MQTT client id, or NATS durable name, or skip the MQTT Session Present check -> the broker creates a fresh cursor and the old backlog is orphaned or silently skipped -> instead reuse the configured identity and verify the broker reports the expected durable state before consuming.

Wrong move: leave idle durable subscriptions in place as if they cost nothing -> brokers must keep per-subscription message references and store files for inactive subscribers (ActiveMQ classic bug reports show broker OOM and KahaDB store-limit overrun driven by stale durable subscribers, and expired messages not released while the subscription exists) -> instead set idle auto-deletion (e.g. autoDeleteOnIdle), unsubscribe on decommission, and alarm on broker store usage.

Wrong move: treat the retention window as unlimited replay storage -> retained (even acknowledged) messages are billed, extend the sensitive-data footprint, and outside the window are discarded regardless of acknowledgement state -> instead size retention to the replay budget, monitor stored bytes, and archive long-horizon history in a system of record rather than the broker.
